footer.projectSummaryText:
This project aims to algorithmically model multiplicative
        hyperrings. It offers a way to experience mathematical
        structures in a computer environment.

home.heroSubtitle:
The "Concretizing Hyperrings" project, supported
          under TÜBİTAK 2209-A
home.heroText:
Our project brings the structure of hyperrings to life in a
          computer environment through a user-friendly algorithm and web
          interface. This lets students and researchers experience abstract
          mathematics firsthand, while also contributing to stronger
          encryption and secure data communication in cybersecurity.
home.exploreHyperringText1:
Hyperrings are an important area of abstract algebra. Unlike
          classical addition and multiplication, a hyperoperation produces a
          set rather than a single element as its result. This property makes
          them especially valuable in fields such as encryption, data
          security, and mathematical modeling.
home.exploreHyperringText2:
First defined in 1934 by F. Marty, hyperrings have a wide range of
          applications in both mathematical theory and applied sciences.
          Thanks to their complex operations, hyperrings can generate unique
          and strong keys, providing extra protection in cybersecurity
          systems.
home.funcAboutText:
Our function is designed to make the structure of hyperrings easy
          to understand. The set elements and rules you enter are processed
          according to the hyperring rules, and if the set satisfies the
          hyperring structure, the results are displayed on screen as a
          table. This way you can explore in practice how hyperrings, a
          theoretical structure, actually work, and better understand how
          these structures can be used in fields such as encryption,
          security, or artificial intelligence.

hyperring.whatText: Hyperrings were first defined by Marty in 1934 and are a subject with a wide range of applications in mathematics. This structure has broad applications in both pure and applied mathematics. Hypergroups, a basic example of hyperrings, are a structure formed when a set H, different from the empty set, is combined with itself, expressed as \( ο \colon H \times H \to P^{*}(H) \), satisfying the union property leading from H to P(H), the collection of non-empty subsets of H. Canonical hypergroups are a special hypergroup defined by Marty.
hyperring.typesText:
Three different types of hyperring have been defined. If only addition “+” is a hyperoperation and multiplication is the classical product, R is called an additive hyperring. A special variant of this type of hyperring was defined by Krasner in 1957. Krasner also defined hyperfields and quotient hyperrings in 1983. On the other hand, if only multiplication is a hyperoperation, this type of hyperring is called a multiplicative hyperring. Multiplicative hyperrings were defined by Rota in 1982. Afterward, many scientists in this field also worked on the subject, including Nakassis (1988), Olson and Ward (1997), and Procesi and Rota (1999). In recent years, algebraic hyperstructures continue to be studied intensively by many mathematicians.
Over the last 15 years, hyperstructures have been shown to have applications in many different fields such as geometry, hypergraphs, fuzzy sets, rough sets, automata theory, cryptography, relation algebras, combinatorics, artificial intelligence, and probability (Corsini & Leoreanu, 2003).
hyperring.defText:
Let there be two binary operations " +" and "." defined on a set R ≠ Ø. The algebraic structure (R, +, .) is called a ring if it satisfies the following conditions:

(1) (R, +) is an abelian group.
(2) "." is associative on R.
(3) "." is left- and right-distributive over "+": for ∀ a,b,c ∈ R, a(b + c) = ab + ac and (a + b)c = ac + bc

The identity element of the ring with respect to "+" is called the ring's zero element and is denoted 0R. The ring may not have an identity element with respect to ".". If it does have an identity element for the second operation, this element is called the ring's unit element and is denoted 1R. Such a ring is also called a ring with identity. Furthermore, if the ring is commutative with respect to the second operation, the ring is called a commutative ring.
hyperring.multText:
This project will primarily focus on hypergroup structures and their multiplication operation. The hypergroup/multiplicative hyperring definition is as follows;
  • When a set H has a hyperoperation ο (mapping a pair of elements to a subset of H), this is called a hypergroupoid.
  • A hypergroupoid is called a semihypergroup if the operation is associative in a specific sense, i.e. (a ο b) ο c = a ο (b ο c).
  • A hypergroupoid is called a quasihypergroup if a ο H = H ο a = H for every a∈H. This condition is known as the reproduction axiom.
  • A hypergroupoid that is both a semihypergroup and a quasihypergroup is called a hypergroup. (F. Marty, 1934, 45-49)
hyperring.cryptoText1:
Because hyperring theory offers more complex structures than
        classical ring and group structures, it provides significant
        advantages in cryptography. Hyperring structures offer a broader set
        of operations than classical ring structures in key generation and
        data encryption processes. This property enables the generation of
        unique and hard-to-predict keys, increasing systems' resilience
        against brute-force or guess-based attacks.
hyperring.cryptoText2:
Hyperring arithmetic makes it possible to generate keys that are
        interlinked through specific mathematical relationships, which makes
        outside interference more difficult. In addition, the non-linear
        transformations offered by hyperring structures make pattern
        analysis harder during data encryption, thereby increasing data
        security.
hyperring.cryptoText3:
When integrated into key-exchange protocols such as Diffie-Hellman,
        hyperring structures create an additional layer of security against
        guess-based and man-in-the-middle attacks. These structures also
        provide flexibility in protocols such as VPN and SSL through dynamic
        key generation.
hyperring.cryptoText4:
Beyond encryption, hyperring-based methods can also be used in data
        integrity protection and digital signature generation. This ensures
        both the confidentiality of data and whether it has been tampered
        with. The algebraic complexity offered by hyperring structures makes
        encryption systems harder to break.
hyperring.cryptoText5:
In conclusion, hyperring structures stand out in cryptography as a
        tool that both increases security and adds flexibility to a system.
        Thanks to their key diversity, non-linear transformations, dynamic
        generation, and data-integrity verification features,
        hyperring-based systems provide a significant advantage in modern
        security protocols.
func.usageIntro:
This function lets you run a hyperring test on the set and rules
          you enter. First, choose whether you want to work on a finite or
          an infinite set.
func.finiteExplain: Finite set: when selected, you need to write the elements separated by commas. (Example: 1,2,3,4)
func.infiniteExplain: Infinite set: when selected, you only need to specify the type of set.
func.ruleSetExplain: If the rule is a set, it must be written in square brackets. Example: [2*a*b, a*b]
func.ruleNormalExplain: If it's a normal rule, you can write it directly. Example: a*b-7
func.resultExplain:
Once the values you entered are processed, the function result
          will be displayed on screen as a table. You can also see which of
          the hyperstructure types the resulting structure matches.

func.rulesLabel: Define Rules ℹ E.g.: a*b or [2*a*b, a*b]

enc.heading: Hyper Encryption Module
enc.infoSystemText: This module demonstrates encryption techniques developed using hyperrings. Unlike classical encryption methods, the hyperring structure provides more complex and secure encryption.
enc.infoModeCustom: Custom Map Mode: Letter-by-letter encryption by customizing keyboard keys
enc.infoModeBinary: Binary Mode: Bit-level encryption by converting text to binary format
enc.infoHow1: Choose a mode with the toggle at the top
enc.infoHow4: Check the result in the preview section
enc.infoTechCustom: Custom Map Mode: Encryption by assigning a custom value to each letter
enc.infoTechBinary: Binary Mode: Bit operations by converting text into 0s and 1s
enc.infoTechRule: Rule System: Custom encryption algorithms via JavaScript functions
enc.customValidationAlert: Please enter a message and assign a key to at least one letter.
enc.chainExplain1: This message was encrypted using the "Cyclic Chaining" method. Each letter is algebraically linked to the next (e.g., a ο b).
enc.chainExplain2: The recipient decrypts the chain in reverse using the hyperstructure rules and matrix resolution (or the known first letter).
enc.chainExplain3: The message has reached the recipient and will be decrypted using the rule '{rule}' and the known key mappings.
enc.chainExplain2b: The recipient knows the rule and the shared key map, and resolves the chain forward starting from the known first value.
enc.decryptAmbiguousNote: (WARNING: the rule isn't injective; the solution shown is one of several possible solutions.)
enc.decryptFailedNote: The chain could not be resolved with this rule and key map (reason: {reason}) -- the rule is not invertible for this chaining.
enc.binaryDecryptExplain: The message has reached the recipient and will be decrypted using the inverse of the rule or known keys.
enc.binaryDecryptExplain2: The recipient re-applies the same bit rule to the encrypted bits; if the rule is involutive (e.g. the default XOR 1), this returns the original.
enc.binaryNotInvolutionNote: (WARNING: this rule is not an involution; re-applying it did not recover the original message.)
mitm.heading: Hyper-DH & Man-In-The-Middle Simulator
mitm.subheading: Simulate communication between Alice and Bob. If Eve (MITM) is active, she intercepts/modifies messages. Click on the nodes.
mitm.aliceHint: Click the Alice monitor — details are shown in the panel.
mitm.bobHint: Click the Bob monitor — details are shown in the panel.
mitm.noNodeSelected: No node selected yet. Click Alice/Bob/Eve.
mitm.footerNote: This simulator runs entirely client-side — it visualizes MITM behavior. For real cryptography, use strong prime numbers and proper libraries.
mitm.infoProtocolText: This simulator demonstrates a Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol developed using hyperrings. Unlike the classical DH protocol, the hyperring structure provides stronger security.
mitm.infoParticipantAlice: Alice: The first party, generates a public key (A) from a private key (a)
mitm.infoParticipantBob: Bob: The second party, generates a public key (B) from a private key (b)
mitm.infoParticipantEve: Eve: The man-in-the-middle attacker, can intercept and modify messages
mitm.infoHow1: Turn Hyper-DH mode on/off (toggle at the top)
mitm.infoHow2: Select Alice or Bob and click "Compute Public Key"
mitm.infoHow3: Once both parties' public keys are computed, the shared secrets are calculated automatically
mitm.infoHow4: Activate Eve to simulate a MITM attack
mitm.infoHow5: Use "Eve: Try Brute Force" to run a real private-key search attack
mitm.infoHow6: Send a message to test the communication
mitm.infoTechModulus: Modulus (p): A prime number, should be large for security
mitm.infoTechGenerator: Generator (g): A primitive root modulo the modulus
mitm.infoTechRule: Rule: Defines the hyperring operation (e.g.: Math.pow(a, b) % n)
